entry.title: From V1 to V2: Transitioning to SAP Sales Cloud & SAP Service Cloud V2 with Confidence
entry.content:
From V1 to V2: Transitioning to SAP Sales Cloud & SAP Service Cloud V2 with Confidence

Moving from SAP Sales Cloud & SAP Service Cloud V1 to V2 is not a routine upgrade. For customers who have spent years building deeply customized processes, it requires careful planning and the right tooling. This article explains what the transition really involves, the questions every customer is asking, and how a set of purpose-built tools makes the journey structured, predictable, and significantly less costly— and addresses the real-world concerns practitioners are raising in the community.

UNDERSTANDING THE SHIFT
This Is Not an Upgrade — It Is a Re-Platforming (And That Is a Good Thing)

The distinction matters. The transition to SAP Sales Cloud & Service Cloud V2 is more than a technology change—it is an opportunity to rethink and modernize how the business operates.

Many customers have built significant business capabilities on SAP Sales Cloud & Service Cloud through PDI-based extensions written in ABSL. As V2 introduces a cloud-native, microservices-based architecture on SAP BTP and follows the Clean Core principle, these customizations do not have a direct lift-and-shift path. Customizations, integrations, and custom business objects therefore need to be assessed and thoughtfully transitioned to the new architecture.

This creates a unique opportunity for customers to step back and ask: What should we carry forward, what can we simplify, and what can we do better? Rather than simply recreating the existing solution, customers can use the transition to:

  • Harmonize business processes and eliminate unnecessary complexity
  • Adopt standard capabilities where V2 has closed the gap
  • Identify where AI and automation can deliver greater efficiency and a better user experience
  • Establish a scalable, maintainable Clean Core foundation for the future

The transition is therefore not just a technical exercise or a rebuild of existing functionality. It is a business transformation opportunity—enabling customers to modernize their processes, preserve what differentiates their business, embrace intelligent capabilities, and build on an architecture designed for the next decade of innovation.

STRUCTURAL CHALLENGES
Three Forces Driving Customer Uncertainty
Customer hesitation around the V1-to-V2 transition is not unwillingness to modernize. It comes from three structural realities that, left unaddressed, make the journey feel complex and costly.

1. Deeply Customized Processes

The vast majority of V1 customers have built custom extensions and business logic that are central to how they operate. These cannot be migrated wholesale — they must be re-engineered, with care taken to preserve competitive differentiation.

2. A Complete Re-Platforming

Moving from monolithic V1 with PDI extensions to V2’s microservices architecture on BTP is not a version bump. Development teams must move from ABSL to CAP Node.js and adopt a fundamentally different extension model.

3. High Cost Without Structure

Without a defined methodology, every project starts from scratch. Cost overruns, timeline uncertainty, and the absence of repeatable patterns stall investment decisions and erode confidence.

THE VOICE OF THE CUSTOMER
The Questions Every Customer Is Asking

Customer conversations at the start of this transition journey consistently surface the same concerns. These are not objections to be managed — they are legitimate questions that deserve concrete answers.

  • Are we looking at a platform change or just a version update?
  • Will our current setup carry over, or does everything need to be rebuilt from scratch?
  • Does moving to V2 mean we lose everything we built in V1?
  • All our custom code and tailored fields — what happens to them?
  • How do we realistically size this in terms of time and budget?
  • Is there a proven path others have followed, or are we on our own?
  • Could this transition be the right moment to bring AI into our day-to-day processes?

TRANSITION ANATOMY
Where the Effort Actually Goes

Understanding how transition effort is distributed helps customers plan resources and set realistic expectations early. The four workstreams below account for the full transition scope.

Workstream

Effort Share

Description

Custom Extensions

40–50%

PDI/ABSL script & CBO transformation to BTP CAP — the single largest effort area

Business Processes

20–30%

Standard feature adoption, UI personalization, configuration and process setup

Integration

~15-20%

Standard and custom integrations

Data Migration

~15-20%

Historical data transfer, validation, and bulk data processing


THE TOOLING ECOSYSTEM
A Purpose-Built Toolkit for Every Phase

SAP has developed a suite of transition tools covering the entire transition lifecycle — from first assessment to go-live. Each tool targets a specific challenge that has historically caused delays or cost overruns. Together, they turn a high-risk, bespoke exercise into a structured, repeatable, and measurably faster process.

1. Pre-Assessment - Parity Check Questionnaire
Structured feature-by-feature comparison of V1 capabilities against V2. Identifies gaps and guides transition scope definition.

The Parity Check Questionnaire provides a structured, feature-by-feature comparison of SAP Sales and Service Cloud V1 capabilities against V2. It helps identify feature gaps, assess feature compatibility, and define the migration scope. By evaluating your current feature usage, the questionnaire helps determine how ready your V1 system is for transition to V2 and highlights areas that may require further assessment or planning.

What you get:

  • Identify the features activated in your current V1 system.
  • Determine whether the features you use in V1 are available in V2.
  • For features not currently available in V2, understand whether they are planned for the product roadmap, helping inform migration decisions and next steps. 

How you get it: available as part of a guided transition engagement. Reach out to your SAP Contact or SAP Professional Services team to get more information.

2. Readiness Check Tool 
Knowing what features exist in V2 is one thing. Knowing whether your organization is actually ready to begin the transition — and what blockers exist — is another.

The Readiness Check Tool evaluates your current V1 landscape — customizations, integrations, data, and processes —Think of it as a health check before you begin.

What you get:

  • See exactly what is in your V1 system — extension fields, PDIs, mashups, and configuration scope
  • Know what moves to V2 automatically, what needs manual work, and what is not supported
  • Functional readiness for V2 transition
  • Walk into planning with a report, not assumptions

How you get it: Available out of the box as standard feature
Readiness Check Tool | SAP Help Portal

3. AssessMate — AI-Powered Extension & Integration Analysis
Manually reviewing hundreds of V1 PDI extensions & integrations to understand complexity, transition effort, and V2 mapping can take weeks and is prone to inconsistency. AssessMate does it in a fraction of the time.

 AssessMate reads it, analyses every custom object and script, and produces a structured report summarizing what you have, how complex it is to move, and what the effort looks like. What used to take a team of experts 10–15 days now takes hours — with consistent, repeatable results every time. In addition to extensions, it also analyzes the integration interfaces as well and gives insights on how these can be migrated to the new V2 landscape.

What you get:

  • A business and technical summary of your V1 extensions & integrations
  • Complexity rating per extension — so you know what is straightforward and what is not
  • Indicative effort estimates to feed your project plan and business case
  • Consistent, AI-driven analysis — not dependent on who does the review
  • A head-start on scoping and stakeholder conversations

 How you get it: available as part of a guided transition engagement. Reach out to your SAP Contact or SAP Professional Services team to get more information.

4. custom code transition tool
Rebuilding V1 custom extensions for V2 is the biggest single cost in any transition — typically 40–50% of total effort. V1 ABSL code has no direct equivalent in V2 and must be completely redesigned. Without automation, this is expensive and slow.

 This is a free AI migration accelerator built on SAP BTP. It reads your V1 ABSL code, understands the business logic behind it, and generates a first-cut V2-ready extension in CAP Node.js — the language V2 uses on SAP BTP. It handles the most time-consuming part: mapping old objects and fields to their V2 equivalents and producing code your developers can review, refine, and deploy. The result is not a finished product, but a validated starting point that eliminates the blank-page problem and dramatically reduces build time. Crucially, it preserves your business logic — so the unique processes your teams rely on survive the move intact.

What you get:

  • AI-generated V2 extension code from your V1 ABSL scripts
  • Automatic mapping of V1 business objects and fields to V2 equivalents
  • Clean Core-compliant output — built for SAP BTP from the start
  • A developer co-pilot that reduces expert hours, not just advice
  • Repeatable, consistent output across every extension in your landscape

 How you get it: SAP Discovery Center Mission - Custom Code Transition Tool for SAP Sales Cloud and SAP Service Cloud

5. custom business object migration tool
Custom business objects — the bespoke data structures your organization built to track unique information — cannot simply be copied across. They need to be fully recreated in V2: data model, screens, and data records.

 This tool automates the migration of custom business objects from V1 to V2 in four guided steps. You provide your V1 object details, and the tool generates the V2 data schema, deploys it on SAP BTP, and includes ready-made UI templates and integration components. What would otherwise require weeks of manual engineering becomes a guided, step-by-step process. Your historical records come across with the structure — nothing is left behind.

What you get:

  • Full data model recreation — no manual schema rebuilding
  • UI screens and BTP integration components included out of the box
  • Your historical records migrated alongside the structure
  • A repeatable, guided process for every custom object in your landscape

How you get it: SAP Discovery Center Mission - Custom Business Object Migration Tool for SAP Sales Cloud and SAP Service Cloud

5. Data Transfer Tool (DTT)
Business process configuration and data migration is where transitions most frequently encounter delays. Manual data migration is error-prone and hard to validate at volume. 

The Data Transfer Tool (DTT) automates the migration of business process configurations, master data (depending on the backend system setup), and transactional data for standard objects from V1 to V2. It also supports the selective migration of specific types of custom fields. DTT enables teams to validate data accuracy and completeness before cutover, reducing the risk of unexpected issues at go-live. It is used during the build phase to perform sample data migrations early and iteratively throughout the project, helping identify and resolve migration issues well in advance.

How you get it: Available out of the box as standard feature
Data Transfer Tool | SAP Help Portal

END-TO-END Transition Journey
A Structured Transition Journey — Six Phases

The tools above are most effective within a structured, phased methodology. Each phase has a clear purpose and the right tools assigned to support it.

  1. Discover & Assess — Parity Check Questionnaire + Readiness Check Tool
  2. Analyze & Plan — AssessMate for deep extension and integration analysis
  3. Explore & Design — Process re-engineering workshops informed by assessment data
  4. Build & Transform — Custom Code Transition Tool + Custom BO Migration Tool
  5. Test & Validate — Data Transfer Tool with iterative testing
  6. Go-Live & Optimize — Cutover, hypercare, and continuous improvement

CUSTOMER TAKEAWAY
What This Means for Your Organization

The tools described here are not just technical accelerators. They change the nature of the transition itself — from unpredictable to planned, from unsupported to guided, from risky to reliable.

01  Plan with confidence
The Parity Check Questionnaire and Readiness Check Tool give you solid facts before you commit a budget or a timeline. AssessMate turns your extension landscape into structured data, not guesswork. You go into planning with a real picture of what you have and what it will take.

02 Move forward with full support
At every phase, there is a tool designed to reduce the dependency on scarce expertise. The Custom Code Transition Tool acts as a co-pilot through the hardest part — custom extension rebuilding. The Custom BO Migration Tool and Data Transfer Tool keep the rest moving. Your team is not alone at any stage.

03 Expect predictable outcomes
AI-assisted analysis gives consistent effort estimates. Automated code generation removes variability from the rebuild phase. Structured workflows mean you know what comes next. The result is a transition you can actually budget for and deliver on time.

04 Transition smoothly — without losing what matters
Your V1 customizations represent years of refinement. The tooling is designed to carry that value forward, not discard it. The custom code transition tool preserves your business logic. The custom BO migration tool brings your data models and records across. You arrive at V2 with your processes intact and your teams ready.

The V1 → V2 transition is also an opportunity — to embed AI into your core processes, rationalize technical debt, and build on an architecture designed for the next decade of innovation. The tooling described here is designed to make sure that opportunity is realized, not deferred.

Ready to take the first step?
Start with the Readiness Check Tool to understand your V1 landscape. Then work with the SAP CX Services team to scope your full transition journey — with data, not guesswork.

Speak to your SAP representative or the SAP CX Services team to get started.

entry.content:
Hello, 

Thank you very much for your question.

Here's the AI-generated response. Please check whether it helps you resolve the issue.

Kind regards,

Henrike

 

Joule Response

SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition: Legacy to Subscription User License Mapping

This is an excellent and highly practical question for sizing and licensing estimation. Based on official SAP documentation and the nested licensing model described for SAP Cloud ERP, here is the most accurate mapping guidance available.

Legacy vs. Subscription User Type Mapping Matrix
Legacy User Type Subscription Equivalent(s) Notes
Self-ServiceSelf-Service (SAP Finance & SCM Self-Service)Direct 1:1 mapping. Covers occasional tasks like time entry, workflow approvals, paystub access.
CoreOperational (primary) + Finance Base + SCM Base (as applicable)Core maps to the "middle tier" of the nested model. Operational is the closest direct equivalent; Finance Base and SCM Base are elevated Core-tier licenses with additional entitlements.
AdvancedFinance Premium + SCM Premium + Finance Base & SCM Base comboAdvanced maps to the highest-capability tiers. Finance Base and SCM Base are NOT Advanced — they sit at the Core tier level.
Key Mapping Clarifications

Core → Subscription Mapping

The legacy Core user type maps to what SAP now calls the "middle tier" of the nested subscription model. Specifically: [1]

  • Operational is the closest direct equivalent to a Core user — covering users engaged in core processes such as sales, inventory, or procurement.
  • Finance Base and SCM Base are also within the Core tier family, but they are elevated versions that include additional entitlements (e.g., SAP Multi-Bank Connectivity, SAP Market Rates Management, SAP Integrated Development) beyond what a plain Operational user receives. [1]
  • The nested model confirms: "a Finance Base User can access everything that an operational user can do and more" — meaning Finance Base ⊃ Operational ⊃ Self-Service. [1]

Practical guidance: A user classified as Core in your TDD environment should be mapped to Operational unless their role specifically requires Finance or SCM Base entitlements. Finance Base and SCM Base are Core-tier licenses, not Advanced.

Advanced → Subscription Mapping

The legacy Advanced user type maps to the Premium tiers in the new subscription model: [1]

  • Finance Premium — includes all Finance Base capabilities plus advanced entitlements (SAP Concur, SAP Ariba, SAP Sales Cloud V2, SAP Project & Resource Management, etc.) [1]
  • SCM Premium — includes all SCM Base capabilities plus advanced sustainability and compliance entitlements (SAP Sustainability Footprint Management, EHS solutions, etc.) [1]
  • Finance Base & SCM Base combo — this combination license is designed for super users needing broad authorization across both Finance and SCM scope areas, and sits at the upper boundary of the Core tier / lower boundary of Advanced. [1]

Critical clarification: Finance Base and SCM Base are NOT Advanced — they are Core-tier licenses. Only Finance Premium and SCM Premium (and the combo) represent the Advanced tier. [1]

The FUE weighting model (used in the legacy RISE model) confirms this hierarchy: 1 FUE = 1 Advanced user, but 1 FUE = 5 Core users — reflecting the significant capability and cost difference. [2] [3]

Sizing & Estimation Guidance

  • Avoid overclassification: Since your TDD environment reports roles as either "Core" or "Advanced," the key risk is mapping all Finance Base / SCM Base users as Advanced. These are Core-tier licenses. Only users requiring Premium-tier entitlements (Concur, Ariba, Sales Cloud V2, EHS, Sustainability tools, etc.) should be classified as Advanced/Premium. [1]

  • Use the IAM Information System app: To proactively identify which business roles and business catalogs map to which price category (Self-Service / Core / Advanced), use the IAM Information System app in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition. Navigate to the Business Role – Business Catalog tab to correlate roles with their pricing category — including at the individual catalog level, not just the role level. [4]

  • Validate via Maintain Business User app: Once roles are assigned, the Maintain Business User app will display the resulting license classification for each user. This allows you to verify the impact before go-live. [5]

  • SAP for Me – License Consumption: You can track licensed FUE/User Subscription quantities and consumption via SAP for Me: Reporting → License Consumption under metric CY334. [6]

  • Official reference: The legally binding user type definitions are in the SAP Cloud ERP Service Use Description, available at the SAP Trust Center. This document provides the authoritative mapping of capabilities per user type. [7]

Summary Mapping at a Glance
 
Self-Service  →  Self-Service (unchanged)
Core          →  Operational (direct match)
                 Finance Base (Core-tier, with Finance entitlements)
                 SCM Base (Core-tier, with SCM entitlements)
Advanced      →  Finance Premium (Advanced-tier)
                 SCM Premium (Advanced-tier)
                 Finance Base & SCM Base Combo (super-user, upper Core/Advanced boundary)

The nested model is the key principle: each higher tier includes all capabilities of the tier below it. Finance Base ⊃ Operational ⊃ Self-Service; Finance Premium ⊃ Finance Base. [1]

  • [5] Users LicenseSAP Community
  • [6] GROW with SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, baseSAP Community
  • [7] Understanding Subscription LicensingSAP Learning

entry.title: Re: Exclude Custom Fields from ORDER_CONFIRMATION_CHANGE
entry.content:
The row with the blank Field Name is a catch all for the whole item line, and that table has no exclude option. In customizing you can only replace it with a list of the fields that must count. I checked and ran it on an S/4HANA 2023 system.

What I measured

  • The rows are in table OMCHGDOC_FIELD, maintained with view OMCD_V1_FIELDV (IMG activity "Assign Output Texts to Document Data"). The key is application object type, output type, table and field name. Besides the key there are only the text ID and the group text ID, no exclude flag. The only table in this area with an exclusion indicator, OMCHGDOC_FILTER, works per receiver, role and channel, and its short text says obsolete.
  • Delivered rows for ORDER_CONFIRMATION_CHANGE in my system: VBAP with blank field, ABGRU, KWMENG, MATNR, NETPR and NETWR; VBAK VDATU; VBEP with blank field, BMENG and EDATU.
  • The check is CL_OM_CHGDOC_UTIL=>CHECK_CHG_TABLE, called from CL_OM_CHGDOC in method IF_CDO_OR_ITEM_VALIDATOR~VALIDATE_OR_ITEM. A row with a field name compares only that field, and only for updated lines. The row with the blank field name does more than follow the update indicator: it reports every inserted or deleted item, and for an updated item it moves the old and the new line into a structure of type VBAP and compares the whole line. Fields from an append on VBAP are components of VBAP, so a change in any custom field counts. There is no BAdI or exit in this check, nor in the classes around it (CL_OM_CHGDOC and CL_OM_CHGDOC_SALES).

I also ran it: I called that method with the delivered rows and an old and a new item line in memory. No sales order was changed and nothing was saved. My system has no custom fields on VBAP, so I changed ARKTX, a standard field that is not in the list and goes through the same code.

  • Only ARKTX changed, delivered rows: changed, reported by the blank VBAP row with update indicator U (text "The item was updated."), and the log of the check names VBAP-ARKTX as the difference.
  • Only ARKTX changed, without the blank VBAP row: not changed.
  • Only KWMENG changed, without the blank VBAP row: changed, through the KWMENG row (text "The item quantity changed.").
  • New item, only the item line: not changed without the blank VBAP row, changed with it (update indicator I, "The item was added.").
  • New item with its schedule line, without the blank VBAP row: changed, through the blank VBEP row ("The schedule line was added.").

What you can do

  • For ORDER_CONFIRMATION_CHANGE, remove the VBAP row with the blank field name and add one row for each VBAP field that must trigger the change output. Your custom fields simply stay out of that list.
  • Side effect: a new or deleted item is then reported through its schedule lines (blank VBEP row), with the schedule line text instead of the item text. An item without schedule lines would not be reported by these table rows on insert or delete.
  • About the delete: in my system the view does not block it. The table has delivery class C, the view has no maintenance restriction, and its only event is a check for new entries. I did not try the delete itself, so if your system refuses it, please post the exact error text.

Use the Maintain Business Roles app and review the restrictions for the business catalog SAP_FIN_BC_APAR_PAY_PC, which controls the Manage Automatic Payments (F0770) app.

You can restrict access by company code and control which payment-processing activities users can perform, such as scheduling payment parameters, proposals and payments.

https://userapps.support.sap.com/sap/support/knowledge/en/3727647

SAP confirms that the restriction type Authorization Group for Supplier works for value help but does not control authorization for payment proposals and payment runs.

Reference: SAP KBA 3631758 – Authorization Group for Supplier only works for value help
https://userapps.support.sap.com/sap/support/knowledge/en/3631758

Therefore, do not rely on supplier authorization groups or payment-run selection parameters as a security control for restricting payments to specific suppliers.

entry.title: onedevatlas is open: one connected graph for SAP developers
entry.content:
Today onedevatlas opens to everyone. It is one connected graph of what is built for SAP development, by SAP and by everyone else: packages, plugins, services, tools, MCP servers and skills, the problems they answer, the posts and talks that explain them, and the people who make them. One graph, read by people and by their agents.

Why it exists

Building has never been easier, and being found has never been harder. On 3 October the atlas listed 31 MCP servers for ABAP. Today it lists 42. Most of them are careful work, and many solve the same problem, because their makers could not see what was already there. Agents make it sharper: an agent knows what it was trained on and what the skills beside it describe, and the work of a freelancer, a partner or a customer team is rarely part of its answer.

The lists we have, for CAP, for UI5, for ABAP, are good and separate. What was missing is a view across the stacks, with SAP's work and the community's side by side, and a graph underneath that says how things relate.

 

A map drawn by capability

Every door, CAP, UI5, ABAP and BTP, and the smaller ones for SAP Commerce, SAP SuccessFactors and SAP Digital Manufacturing, has its own map. One hexagon is one capability, a concern a project has, and its colour says who is present: SAP, the community, both, or nobody yet. Open a tile and the capability page says what SAP ships, where that stops, and who else is present. Under a capability, use cases make the options comparable by the outcome they cover and the conditions under which they cover it, never by stars or downloads.

Behind the map is the graph itself, at /graph: select a node and its card says what it provides, who maintains it and what it depends on, each edge with one meaning.

The same answers for your agent

The hosted MCP server at https://onedevatlas.dev/mcp answers with the same facts the pages show. This exchange was recorded against the live server today: a question about letting a coding agent change ABAP in an on-premise system lands on a capability, then on an assessed use case with seven options, six covering it under conditions and one not known, and the four things that decide between them for your system.

Explore, and TechEd week

The third way in is a flight. Explore and Play is the same graph as a place: make an orb, design a ship and fly through the ecosystems. Until Sunday 1 November, midnight in Berlin, it is shared: sign in with GitHub, meet other pilots, play rock, paper, scissors (SAP style) and collect points for what you look at. Then the boards freeze, and the leaders stay in the atlas's history.

 

Take part

If your work is missing or something about it is wrong, open an issue. Anything about a person goes directly through the contact form. Maintainers can sign in and write a note on their own entry.

The full article explains the words the atlas uses and how to read a capability page, and its discussion is open.

See you at TechEd, or in flight. 🚀

entry.title: Re: Inflated G/L account balances resulting from clearing...
entry.content:
Hello @xuqi_fangaf39f1 

In SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, this is generally standard accounting behavior.

The Debit and Credit Transaction Figures in the Display G/L Account Balances app represent the total debit and credit turnover for the selected period, not just the closing balance.

When a clearing document contains new G/L postings, those debit and credit amounts are added to the transaction figures. For example:

Original posting 1,000 Dr  1,000 Cr
Clearing document 1,000 Dr 1,000 Cr
Total transaction figures 2,000 Dr 2,000 Cr

Although the debit and credit transaction figures increase, the net balance remains unchanged. This is expected when the clearing document contains offsetting postings.

Can this be prevented?

There is no standard setting to exclude posted clearing-document line items from G/L transaction figures. The accounting records must reflect the postings that have occurred.

entry.title: SAP EarlyWatch Alert: A Unified View of Missing Side-Effect Solving Notes
entry.content:
Introduction

Maintaining the stability and reliability of SAP systems involves more than implementing SAP Notes to resolve known issues. In some cases, an implemented SAP Note may introduce a known side effect that requires a corresponding side-effect solving SAP Note.

Identifying missing side-effect solving SAP Notes is essential for assessing potential risks and determining appropriate corrective actions. The SAP EarlyWatch Alert Service helps customers address this challenge by detecting missing solving notes and triggering alerts for affected systems. However, locating and reviewing this information can be challenging when the findings are spread across multiple system components and different sections of the SAP EarlyWatch Alert Report.

To make this process easier, a new functionality is available in the SAP EarlyWatch Alert experience for on-premise and private cloud systems.

What's New?

Get the complete picture at a glance! A new card in the Support tab of the System Details page in SAP for Me now provides a consolidated list of missing side-effect solving SAP Notes identified by the SAP EarlyWatch Alert Service across your system's components—making it easier to spot potential issues, gain insights, and take action.

No more piecing together information from different sources! Previously, these details were scattered across individual components in the SAP EarlyWatch Alert Solution Finder results and various sections of the SAP EarlyWatch Alert Report.

With this enhancement, users can access the relevant information in one place instead of navigating through multiple components and report sections to build a complete picture.

Where Can You Find the New Overview?

The functionality is available for on-premise and private cloud systems.

To access the overview:

  1. Open the relevant system's System Details page under Systems and Provisioning in SAP for Me.
  2. Navigate to the Support tab.
  3. Locate the new card for missing side-effect solving notes.
  4. Review the consolidated findings across the system's components.

This provides a convenient starting point for understanding which missing notes have been identified and may require attention.

Which Components Are Covered?

The functionality covers the components evaluated by the SAP EarlyWatch Alert Service for missing side-effect solving SAP Notes. The applicable component coverage and exclusions depend on the supported checks and system type.

For a detailed list of the components included in the checks, as well as those excluded from the overview, refer to SAP Note 3362629 – Missing Side Effects Solving SAP Notes Detected by SAP EarlyWatch Alert Service.

 

How Can You Use This Information?

The consolidated overview helps you identify missing side-effect solving SAP Notes and prioritize further investigation.

When reviewing the findings, consider the following steps:

  1. Review the missing notes listed for your system.
  2. Examine the corresponding SAP Notes and their relevance to the affected components.
  3. Assess the potential impact on your system and business processes.
  4. Determine the appropriate corrective actions based on the applicable SAP Note instructions and your system's requirements.

The overview supports your analysis and decision-making. The relevance of each finding should be assessed in the context of your individual system before implementing any changes.

“Spot missing  SAP Notes. Stay ahead of side effects.”!

entry.title: SAPAutoLogon: Connect KeePass with SAP Logon and SAP GUI
entry.content:
Introduction

Anyone who works with many SAP systems keeps logon details somewhere: system ID, application server, instance number, client, user and password. A password manager is the right place for the credentials, but the connection data is usually typed again by hand, or the session is started through SAP Logon in a separate step.

SAPAutoLogon brings both together. It is a free, open source plugin for KeePass 2.x that reads your SAP Logon configuration, fills the connection fields of a KeePass entry, and starts SAP GUI or SAP Business Client directly from the KeePass entry list.

  Importing a SAP Logon folder into a KeePass group.

What the plugin does

SAP tab in the entry dialog. The Add Entry and Edit Entry dialogs get an additional SAP tab. In Manual mode, which is the default, you enter the connection fields yourself and a status line tells you whether the entry is ready to launch.

 The SAP tab in Manual mode.

In Automatic mode a searchable list shows the systems from SAP Logon. Selecting one fills the fields, and every field stays editable. Direct application servers, logon groups with a message server, SAProuter strings and SNC are supported. If SAP Logon stores no client or language, the plugin fills client 100 and language EN.

  The SAP tab in Automatic mode, with the search box and the selected system.

The values are stored as normal string fields of the entry (systemId, applicationServer, systemNumber, messageServer, messageServerPort, group, sapRouterString, sncName, sncType, client, language and transaction). They are visible on the Advanced tab, and the database stays readable without the plugin.

Import from SAP Logon. The context menu of a KeePass group has the command Import from SAP Logon.

  The group context menu with the Import from SAP Logon command.

A window shows the SAP Logon folder tree with the number of systems per folder, a search box and a preview of what will be created. Subfolders become nested groups and systems become entries. Existing groups are reused, and entries that are already present are skipped and never changed. You can optionally set a default user name for systems that have none in SAP Logon. Imported entries receive the SAP logo as their icon.

  The Import from SAP Logon window.

Launching. The columns SAP GUI and Business Client in the entry list start the session with a double click. The same actions are in the entry context menu and on the shortcuts Ctrl+Shift+G for SAP GUI and Ctrl+Shift+N for SAP Business Client. SAP GUI is started through sapshcut.exe, whose parameters are described in SAP Note 103019, and SAP Business Client through NWBC.exe.

  Imported groups and entries with the launch columns.

Installation

  1. Download SAPAutoLogon.dll from the latest release on GitHub.
  2. Copy it into the Plugins folder of your KeePass installation.
  3. Restart KeePass.
  4. The SAP GUI and Business Client columns appear in the entry list automatically.

Requirements are Windows, KeePass 2.x, SAP GUI for Windows with sapshcut.exe and/or SAP Business Client, and SAP Logon for the system list. Without SAP Logon the SAP tab still works in Manual mode. If you used another SAP launch plugin before, remove it first. The plugin supports the KeePass update check under Help, Check for Updates.

Security considerations

Please read this section before you use the plugin with productive systems.

  • The plugin only reads the SAP Logon landscape files, including the shared landscape file, and never changes them or the registry. If the shared landscape is configured as a URL, it is fetched with a plain GET request. There is no other network access and no telemetry.
  • To log on automatically, the user name and the password of the KeePass entry are passed to sapshcut.exe as arguments. The password is therefore visible on the command line of the process while SAP GUI starts. This is how sapshcut.exe works, so decide for each system whether this is acceptable.
  • The optional default user name of the import is stored in plain text in KeePass.config.xml. Never enter a password there.
  • An import changes the database in memory. KeePass has no undo, so review the result before you save.

Source, download and feedback

  • Project page with screenshots: https://abgunes.github.io/SAPAutoLogon/
  • Source code and download (AGPL 3.0): https://github.com/abgunes/SAPAutoLogon

The plugin builds on the KPSAPLunch plugin by David Suchopar. I would be glad to hear which connection types and SAP Logon setups you use, so please leave a comment or open an issue on GitHub.

#SAP GUI, #SAPLogon, #SAPBusinessClient, #KeePass, #Security

entry.title: Re: CNIF_STATUS001 BAPI_BUS2054_SET_STATUS Resetting status &1 for object &2 not supported
entry.content:
The system status CRTD cannot be removed.

BAPI_BUS2054_SET_STATUS calls the subroutine CNIF_SYSTEM_STATUS_2054_CHECK to do the check of allowed system statuses, CRTD is not one of them:

FORM cnif_system_status_2054_check
                 USING    p_status   TYPE bapi_system_status_text
                          p_mode     TYPE bapi_status_action
                 CHANGING p_allowed  TYPE boole_d.

  p_allowed = false.

  CASE p_status.
    WHEN 'REL' OR 'REL '.
      IF p_mode = 'S'.
        p_allowed = true.
      ENDIF.
    WHEN 'LKD' OR 'LKD '.
      p_allowed = true.
    WHEN 'TECO'.
      p_allowed = true.
    WHEN 'CLSD'.
      p_allowed = true.
    WHEN 'AALK'.
      p_allowed = true.
    WHEN 'MDLK'.
      p_allowed = true.
    WHEN 'DLFL'.
      p_allowed = true.
    WHEN 'DDLK'.              "++3230129
      p_allowed = true.
    WHEN 'PLLK'.
      p_allowed = true.
    WHEN 'BMLK'.
      p_allowed = true.      "--3230129
    WHEN space.              " no value  provided
      p_allowed = true.
  ENDCASE..

ENDFORM.

Code of BAPI_BUS2054_SET_STATUS:

  loop at I_WBS_SYSTEM_STATUS.
    if not i_wbs_system_status-undo_system_status is initial.
      PERFORM cnif_system_status_2054_check
                  USING I_WBS_SYSTEM_STATUS-undo_system_status
                        c_U
                  CHANGING
                        l_check_ok.
      IF l_check_ok = false.
        CALL FUNCTION 'METHOD_START_LOG'
          EXPORTING
            METHOD     = c_check
            OBJ_TYP    = CO1_TYPE-wbs_element
            OBJ_ID_EXT = I_WBS_SYSTEM_STATUS-wbs_element
          IMPORTING
            LOG_LEVEL  = LOG_LEVEL.
        message E001(CNIF_STATUS)
                WITH I_WBS_SYSTEM_STATUS-UNDO_SYSTEM_STATUS
                     I_WBS_SYSTEM_STATUS-WBS_ELEMENT
                     INTO NULL.

Don't try to undo the system status CRTD.

Sandra

PS: code is S/4HANA 2023 FPS 01
